Particle systems

We define two state spaces for two versions of our Markov dynamics.

Definition 2.3

The vertex model state space is2.14\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \mathscr {G}:=\biggl \{ \textbf{g}=(g_1,g_2,\ldots ):g_i\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0},\ \sum _{i=1}^{\infty }g_i<\infty \biggr \}. \end{aligned}$$\end{document}G:={g=(g1,g2,…):gi∈Z≥0,∑i=1∞gi<∞}.The last condition means that only finitely many of the \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_i$$\end{document}gi’s are nonzero.

The exclusion process state space is2.15\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \mathscr {X}:=\Bigl \{ \textbf{x}= \left( x_1>x_2>x_3>\ldots \right) :x_i\in \mathbb {Z}, \ \, x_n=-n \ \text {for all sufficiently large { n}} \Bigr \}.\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$\end{document}X:={x=x1>x2>x3>…:xi∈Z,xn=-nfor all sufficiently largen}.We view \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}$$\end{document}x as a particle configuration in \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathbb {Z}$$\end{document}Z, which is empty far to the right and densely packed far to the left. In other words, every \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}\in \mathscr {X}$$\end{document}x∈X differs from the distinguished step configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}_{step}:=\left\{ -1>-2>-3>\ldots \right\} $$\end{document}xstep:=-1>-2>-3>… by finitely many particle jumps to the right by one, when a particle may only jump to an unoccupied location.

Definition 2.4

(Gap-particle transformation). Let the (well-known) bijection \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X} \rightarrow \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}X→G with \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x} \mapsto \textbf{g}$$\end{document}x↦g be defined as2.16\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} g_i=x_{i}-x_{i+1}-1,\qquad i\ge 1; \end{aligned}$$\end{document}gi=xi-xi+1-1,i≥1;see Fig. 7 for an illustration. Additionally, we use the convention \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_0=x_0=+\infty $$\end{document}g0=x0=+∞, which extends (2.16) to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i=0$$\end{document}i=0.

We refer to (2.16) as the gap-particle transformation. Note, in particular, that the distinguished step configuration of particles, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}_{step}$$\end{document}xstep, corresponds to the empty configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}_{step}:=(0,0,\ldots )$$\end{document}gstep:=(0,0,…). In the special case, when the updates are parallel and not sequential, this is the same as the zero range process (ZRP) / ASEP transformation, e.g., see [Pov13].

We are now in a position to describe the fused stochastic higher spin six vertex (FS6V) model \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t) and its exclusion process counterpart, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}(t)$$\end{document}x(t). Both models were introduced in [CP16b] for homogeneous parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$u_i\equiv u$$\end{document}ui≡u, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_i\equiv s$$\end{document}si≡s, and their inhomogeneous versions were considered in [BP18a]. Here and throughout the rest of the section, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}t∈Z≥0 stands for discrete time in \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t).

The time-homogeneous Markov process \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\textbf{g}(t)\}_{t\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}}$$\end{document}{g(t)}t∈Z≥0 on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {G}$$\end{document}G depends on two sequences of parameters2.17\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \textbf{s}=(s_0,s_1,s_2,\ldots ),\quad s_i\in (-1,0]; \qquad \textbf{u}=(u_0,u_1,u_2,\ldots ),\quad u_i\in [0,+\infty ), \nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$\end{document}s=(s0,s1,s2,…),si∈(-1,0];u=(u0,u1,u2,…),ui∈[0,+∞),as well as on the parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q\in [0,1)$$\end{document}q∈[0,1) and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$J \in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 1}$$\end{document}J∈Z≥1, as in (2.7). For convergence reasons discussed in Lemma 2.6 below, we assume that2.18\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \frac{(-s_i)(u_i-s_i)}{1-u_is_i}<1-\varepsilon <1 \end{aligned}$$\end{document}(-si)(ui-si)1-uisi<1-ε<1for some fixed \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\varepsilon >0$$\end{document}ε>0 and all i large enough. For future use, let us write \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(\textbf{u},\textbf{s})\in \mathcal {T}$$\end{document}(u,s)∈T if the parameters satisfy the conditions (2.17)–(2.18).

Remark 2.5

One readily sees that if \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$-1<s_i< 0$$\end{document}-1<si<0 and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$u_i>0$$\end{document}ui>0, then \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\frac{(-s_i)(s_i-u_i)}{1-s_iu_i}< 1$$\end{document}(-si)(si-ui)1-siui<1. The condition (2.18) is stronger than (2.17) in that it does not allow these ratios to get arbitrarily close to 1 as i goes to infinity.

Let us describe how to randomly update the FS6V model \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t) in (discrete) time t. Fix time \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}t∈Z≥0, set \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}=\textbf{g}(t)\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g=g(t)∈G, and let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'=\textbf{g}(t+1)\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g′=g(t+1)∈G be the random update. The update is independent of time t and occurs as follows:2.19\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} g_i' = g_i+h_{i-1}-h_i, \qquad i=1,2,\ldots , \end{aligned}$$\end{document}gi′=gi+hi-1-hi,i=1,2,…,so that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_i \in \left\{ 0,1,\ldots ,J \right\} $$\end{document}hi∈0,1,…,J, with \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}i∈Z≥0, are random variables that are sampled sequentially using the stochastic vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u_i,s_i}$$\end{document}Lui,si(J) for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i=0,1,2,\ldots $$\end{document}i=0,1,2,…. Namely, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_0$$\end{document}h0 is sampled from the probability distribution \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u_0,s_0}(\infty ,0;\infty ,h_0)$$\end{document}Lu0,s0(J)(∞,0;∞,h0) (2.13). Then sequentially for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i=1,2,\ldots $$\end{document}i=1,2,…, given \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_{i-1}$$\end{document}hi-1 and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_i$$\end{document}gi, we sample the pair \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(g_i',h_i)$$\end{document}(gi′,hi) with \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_i'+h_i=g_i+h_{i-1}$$\end{document}gi′+hi=gi+hi-1 from the probability distribution \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u_i,s_i}(g_i,h_{i-1};g_i',h_{i})$$\end{document}Lui,si(J)(gi,hi-1;gi′,hi) (2.8). Below, in Lemma 2.6, we show that eventually the update terminates, making it well-defined.

Lemma 2.6

We have \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_i=0$$\end{document}hi=0 for all i large enough for the update (2.19) with probability 1.

Proof

We know that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_i=0$$\end{document}gi=0 for all i large enough. Since \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u,s}(0,0;0,0)=1$$\end{document}Lu,s(J)(0,0;0,0)=1, it suffices to note that all the probabilities of the form \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u_i,s_i}(0,j;0,j)=\frac{s_i^{2j}(u_i/s_i;q)_j}{(s_iu_i;q)_j}$$\end{document}Lui,si(J)(0,j;0,j)=si2j(ui/si;q)j(siui;q)j, where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$j \in \left\{ 0,1,\ldots ,J \right\} $$\end{document}j∈0,1,…,J, are bounded away from 1 uniformly in \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$j\ge 1$$\end{document}j≥1 and sufficiently large i, due to (2.18). This means that once i becomes large enough so that all further \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_i$$\end{document}gi’s are zero, then with probability 1 the quantities \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_i$$\end{document}hi eventually decrease to zero, and the update terminates. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

After the sequential update over \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i=0,1,\ldots $$\end{document}i=0,1,… terminates according to Lemma 2.6, we have reached the next state \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'=\textbf{g}(t+1)$$\end{document}g′=g(t+1).

The trajectory of the Markov process \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\left\{ \textbf{g}(t) \right\} _{t\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}}$$\end{document}g(t)t∈Z≥0 may be viewed as a random path ensemble in the quadrant \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathbb {Z}_{\ge 1}^{2}$$\end{document}Z≥12. Namely, the initial condition \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(0)$$\end{document}g(0) corresponds to the paths entering the quadrant from below, and the quantities \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_0$$\end{document}h0 sampled at each time moment \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t\ge 1$$\end{document}t≥1 determine the paths entering from the left. The configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g(t)∈G describes the paths crossing the horizontal line at height \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t+\frac{1}{2}$$\end{document}t+12. The random update from \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t) to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t+1)$$\end{document}g(t+1) determines the horizontal path counts at height \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t+1$$\end{document}t+1. See Fig. 7 for an illustration.

Denote by \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Tu,s the one-step Markov transition operator for the FS6V process \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\textbf{g}(t)\}_{t\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}}$$\end{document}{g(t)}t∈Z≥0 on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {G}$$\end{document}G. This operator also depends on the parameters q and J, but we suppress this in the notation. In the literature on solvable lattice models (for instance, [Bax07]), \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Tu,s is often referred to as the transfer matrix. Our transfer matrix is a Markov transition operator since the model is stochastic. Finally, let us describe the Markov process \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\textbf{x}(t)\}_{t\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}}$$\end{document}{x(t)}t∈Z≥0 on the space \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X induced by the FS6V process \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\left\{ \textbf{g}(t) \right\} $$\end{document}g(t) via the gap-particle transformation (2.16). The random update from \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}(t)$$\end{document}x(t) to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}(t+1)$$\end{document}x(t+1) is described as follows. First, the rightmost particle \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_1$$\end{document}x1 jumps to the right by a random distance \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_0$$\end{document}h0 sampled from \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u_0,s_0}(\infty ,0;\infty ,h_0)$$\end{document}Lu0,s0(J)(∞,0;∞,h0) (2.13). Then, sequentially for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i=1,2,\ldots $$\end{document}i=1,2,…, the particle \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_{i+1}$$\end{document}xi+1 jumps to the right by a random distance \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_i$$\end{document}hi sampled from\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} L^{(J)}_{u_i,s_i}(x_i(t)-x_{i+1}(t)-1,h_{i-1};x_{i}(t+1)-x_{i+1}(t+1)-1,h_i), \end{aligned}$$\end{document}Lui,si(J)(xi(t)-xi+1(t)-1,hi-1;xi(t+1)-xi+1(t+1)-1,hi),given that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_{i}$$\end{document}xi has jumped by the distance \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_{i-1}$$\end{document}hi-1. Note that the upper bound for the distance of each particle’s jump is equal to the parameter J.

Due to the path conservation, we see that the dynamics of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}(t)$$\end{document}x(t) satisfies the exclusion rule, that is, a particle may only jump to an unoccupied location. Consequently, the strict order of the particles \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_1>x_2>\ldots $$\end{document}x1>x2>… is preserved throughout the dynamics. We also note that the jump of each particle \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_i$$\end{document}xi at time t is governed by the parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(u_{i-1},s_{i-1})$$\end{document}(ui-1,si-1) as well as the locations \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_i(t)$$\end{document}xi(t), \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_{i-1}(t)$$\end{document}xi-1(t), and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_{i-1}(t+1)$$\end{document}xi-1(t+1).

We denote the one-step Markov transition operator of the process \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\textbf{x}(t)\}_{t\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}}$$\end{document}{x(t)}t∈Z≥0 on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X by \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{T}_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}T~u,s. It is the image of the FS6V model operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Tu,s on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {G}$$\end{document}G under the gap-particle transformation (2.16). Throughout the paper we adopt the same convention for all Markov transition operators: A on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {G}$$\end{document}G corresponds to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{A}$$\end{document}A~ on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X.

Yang-Baxter Equation and Cross Vertex Weights

The vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u,s}$$\end{document}Lu,s(J) (2.8) satisfy the Yang-Baxter equation, and this makes the stochastic processes from Sections 2 very special, i.e., integrable. In short, the Yang-Baxter equation determines the (local) action of swapping two consecutive vertex weights in the FS6V model. This swapping action is represented by introducing a cross-vertex that is dragged across the vertex weights; see Fig. 9.

Vertical Yang-Baxter equation

There are several possible Yang-Baxter equations that the vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u,s}$$\end{document}Lu,s(J)’s may satisfy. For our purposes, we focus on the Yang-Baxter equation that may be represented by vertically dragging a cross vertex through two consecutive horizontal vertex weights.

Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_1,s_2\in (-1,0]$$\end{document}s1,s2∈(-1,0] and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$z\ge 0$$\end{document}z≥0 be three parameters. The vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u,s}$$\end{document}Lu,s(J) and the cross vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{z,s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Rz,s1,s2 satisfy the following Yang-Baxter equation:

Proposition 3.1

[Yang-Baxter equation]. Fix the path counts \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_1,j_1 \in \left\{ 0,1,\ldots ,J \right\} $$\end{document}i1,j1∈0,1,…,J, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_2,i_3,j_2,j_3\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}i2,i3,j2,j3∈Z≥0 and the parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$u_1,u_2,s_1,s_2$$\end{document}u1,u2,s1,s2. Then, we have3.3\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \begin{aligned}&\sum _{k_1,k_2,k_3} R_{\frac{u_2}{u_1},s_1,s_2}(j_3,k_2;k_3,j_2) \hspace{1pt}L^{(J)}_{u_1,s_1}(i_2,i_1;k_2,k_1) \hspace{1pt}L^{(J)}_{u_2,s_2}(i_3,k_1;k_3,j_1) \\&\quad = \sum _{k_1,k_2,k_3} L^{(J)}_{u_2,s_2}(k_3,i_1;j_3,k_1)\hspace{1pt}L^{(J)}_{u_1,s_1}(k_2,k_1;j_2,j_1)\hspace{1pt}R_{\frac{u_2}{u_1},s_1,s_2}(k_3,i_2;i_3,k_2). \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$\end{document}∑k1,k2,k3Ru2u1,s1,s2(j3,k2;k3,j2)Lu1,s1(J)(i2,i1;k2,k1)Lu2,s2(J)(i3,k1;k3,j1)=∑k1,k2,k3Lu2,s2(J)(k3,i1;j3,k1)Lu1,s1(J)(k2,k1;j2,j1)Ru2u1,s1,s2(k3,i2;i3,k2).See Fig. 9 for an illustration. The sums in (3.3) are over \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$k_1 \in \left\{ 0,1,\ldots ,J \right\} $$\end{document}k1∈0,1,…,J and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$k_2,k_3\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}k2,k3∈Z≥0. However, both sum are finite due to the path conservation properties, making the Yang-Baxter equation (3.3) an identity between rational functions.

Observe that the cross vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{\frac{u_2}{u_1},s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Ru2u1,s1,s2 entering the Yang-Baxter equation (3.3) do not depend on the parameter J and only depend on the parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$u_1,u_2$$\end{document}u1,u2 through their ratio.

Proof of Proposition 3.1

The Yang-Baxter equation (3.3) follows by fusion from the simpler case when the paramters are \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_1=s_2=q^{-1/2}$$\end{document}s1=s2=q-1/2 and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$I_1=1$$\end{document}I1=1. This simpler case of the Yang-Baxter equation may be checked through direct computations. Moreover, the latter equation essentially coincides with [BMP21, Proposition A.1], up to the specialization of their parameter s into \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q^{-J/2}$$\end{document}q-J/2 and a gauge transformation making the vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$w_{u,s}$$\end{document}wu,s stochastic. Note that the cross vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$r_{u/v}$$\end{document}ru/v in [BMP21, Proposition A.1] are already stochastic (i.e. satisfy the sum to one property). Then, our fused Yang-Baxter equation (3.3) follows from [BMP21, Proposition A.3] (which is essentially a fusion of [BMP21, Proposition A.1]), up to a gauge transformation and path complementation \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i\mapsto I-i$$\end{document}i↦I-i.

Alternatively, the fused Yang-Baxter equation with stochastic vertex weights implying (3.3) is a color-blind case of the master Yang-Baxter equation coming from \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak {sl}_n})$$\end{document}Uq(sln^) obtained in [BM16]; see [BW22, (C.1.2)]. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

Nonnegativity

From Proposition 2.1, we see that the cross vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{z,s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Rz,s1,s2, defined by (3.1), satisfy the sum to one property3.4\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \sum _{i_1,j_2=0}^{\infty } R_{z,s_1,s_2}(i_1,i_2;j_1,j_2)=1 \end{aligned}$$\end{document}∑i1,j2=0∞Rz,s1,s2(i1,i2;j1,j2)=1for any fixed \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_2,j_1\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}i2,j1∈Z≥0. Moreover, if the vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{z,s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Rz,s1,s2 are nonnegative, the vertex weights define a probability distribution. This distribution is on the top paths \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(i_1, j_2)$$\end{document}(i1,j2) of a cross vertex for any fixed bottom paths \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(i_2,j_1)$$\end{document}(i2,j1), see Fig. 8. Below, we show that the cross vertex weights are nonnegative under a suitable restriction of the parameters.

For \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_1\ne i_2$$\end{document}i1≠i2, one can check that conditions \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_1,s_2\in (-1,0)$$\end{document}s1,s2∈(-1,0) and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$0\le z\le \min \{\frac{s_1}{s_2},\frac{s_2}{s_1}\}$$\end{document}0≤z≤min{s1s2,s2s1} are enough for nonnegativity since only the first summand in (3.11) is present. When \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_1=i_2$$\end{document}i1=i2, in the second summand in (3.11) we have \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_2z-s_1\ge 0$$\end{document}s2z-s1≥0, so the second summand is negative. Combining it with the first summand leads to the additional condition \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_1^2+s_2^2 \le 1+zs_1s_2$$\end{document}s12+s22≤1+zs1s2. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

Specialization to q-beta-binomial cross vertex weights

For \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q>0$$\end{document}q>0, the cross vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{\frac{u_2}{u_1},s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Ru2u1,s1,s2 (3.2) have a complicated q-hypergeometric expression, even when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$J=1$$\end{document}J=1 and the lattice vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u_i,s_i}$$\end{document}Lui,si(J) entering the Yang-Baxter equation (3.3) are explicit rational functions (see (2.11)). There are several ways to specialize the cross vertex parameters to simplify \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{\frac{u_2}{u_1},s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Ru2u1,s1,s2. For instance, one may take finite spin specializations by setting, in the simplest case, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_1=s_2=q^{-\frac{1}{2}}$$\end{document}s1=s2=q-12. However, this specialization would bound the gap sizes in the higher spin exclusion process \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}(t)$$\end{document}x(t) defined in Sect. 2.3 and, as a result, we will not consider this specialization here. Instead, we distinguish a specialization reducing \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{\frac{u_2}{u_1},s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Ru2u1,s1,s2 to the q-beta-binomial distribution:

Proposition 3.5

If \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$u_2/u_1=s_2/s_1$$\end{document}u2/u1=s2/s1, then the cross vertex weights in the Yang-Baxter equation in Proposition 3.1 are simplified as3.16\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} R_{\frac{s_2}{s_1},s_1,s_2} (i_1,i_2;j_1,j_2) = \textbf{1}_{i_1+j_2=i_2+j_1} \cdot \textbf{1}_{j_2\le j_1} \cdot \varphi _{q,s_2^2/s_1^2,s_2^2}(j_2\mid j_1), \end{aligned}$$\end{document}Rs2s1,s1,s2(i1,i2;j1,j2)=1i1+j2=i2+j1·1j2≤j1·φq,s22/s12,s22(j2∣j1),where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\varphi _{q,s_2^2/s_1^2,s_2^2}$$\end{document}φq,s22/s12,s22 is the q-beta-binomial distribution (2.3).

Proof

This is a combination of (3.1) and the reduction of the weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{s,s}$$\end{document}Ls,s(J) (2.12). Here we set \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q^{I_1}=s_1^{-2}$$\end{document}qI1=s1-2. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

Recall (2.5) and note that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{\frac{s_2}{s_1},s_1,s_2} (i_1,i_2;j_1,j_2)\ge 0$$\end{document}Rs2s1,s1,s2(i1,i2;j1,j2)≥0 for all \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_1,i_2,j_1,j_2\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}i1,i2,j1,j2∈Z≥0 if3.17\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} s_1,s_2 \in (-1,0],\qquad |s_2|\le |s_1|. \end{aligned}$$\end{document}s1,s2∈(-1,0],|s2|≤|s1|.We see that the specialization \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$z=s_2/s_1$$\end{document}z=s2/s1 extends the range of nonnegativity of the cross vertex weights compared to the conditions of Proposition 3.2. Limit to infinitely many paths

We will also need a limit of the cross vertex weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$R_{z,s_1,s_2}(i_1,i_2;j_1,j_2)$$\end{document}Rz,s1,s2(i1,i2;j1,j2) as the number of southwest incoming paths \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_2$$\end{document}i2 grows to infinity:

Proposition 3.7

Intertwining Relations

In this section we present our first main result, the intertwining (or quasi-commutation) relations for the Markov transition operator of the stochastic higher spin six vertex model. Here we discuss the result at the level of Markov operators based on vertex weights. Then, in Sects. 5 and 6 below, we present its specializations to exclusion processes on the line, such as q-TASEP and TASEP, and to the Schur vertex model.

Remark 4.3

In (4.2) and throughout the paper, we adopt the convention that the product of Markov operators follows the order of their action on measures. In particular, on arbitrary delta measures \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\delta _{\textbf{g}}$$\end{document}δg, where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g∈G is fixed, the identity (4.2) is expanded as follows4.3\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \sum _{\textbf{g}'\in \mathscr {G}} T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}} (\textbf{g},\textbf{g}') \hspace{1pt}P^{(n)}_{u_n/u_{n-1},s_{n-1},s_n} (\textbf{g}',\textbf{g}'') = \sum _{\hat{\textbf{g}}'\in \mathscr {G}} P^{(n)}_{u_n/u_{n-1},s_{n-1},s_n} (\textbf{g},\hat{\textbf{g}}') \hspace{1pt}T_{\sigma _{n-1}\textbf{u},\sigma _{n-1}\textbf{s}} (\hat{\textbf{g}}',\textbf{g}''),\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$\end{document}∑g′∈GTu,s(g,g′)Pun/un-1,sn-1,sn(n)(g′,g′′)=∑g^′∈GPun/un-1,sn-1,sn(n)(g,g^′)Tσn-1u,σn-1s(g^′,g′′),for any fixed \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{g}''\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g,g′′∈G; see Fig. 10 for an illustration. Lemma 4.6

If \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(\textbf{u},\textbf{s})\in \mathcal {B}$$\end{document}(u,s)∈B, then the shift operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$B_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Bu,s is well-defined.

Proof

Since \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(u_n/u_0,s_0,s_n)\in \mathcal {R}$$\end{document}(un/u0,s0,sn)∈R for all \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$n\ge 1$$\end{document}n≥1, all vertex weights involved in the operators \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}_{u_n/u_0,s_0,s_n}$$\end{document}Pun/u0,s0,sn(n) in the product (4.6) are nonnegative. Next, the second condition in (4.5) implies that no path escapes to infinity under the action of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$B_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Bu,s, similarly to the proof of Lemma 2.6. Indeed, we have\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} R_{\frac{u_n}{u_0},s_0,s_n}(0,j;0,j)=\frac{s_n^{2j}(u_ns_0/(u_0s_n);q)_{j}}{(u_ns_0s_n/u_0;q)_{j}}, \qquad j \in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}, \end{aligned}$$\end{document}Runu0,s0,sn(0,j;0,j)=sn2j(uns0/(u0sn);q)j(uns0sn/u0;q)j,j∈Z≥0,and due to (4.5), these quantities are bounded away from 1 uniformly in \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$j\ge 1$$\end{document}j≥1 for all n sufficiently large. This completes the proof. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

The first main structural result is the next Theorem 4.7. It concerns the stochastic higher spin six vertex model \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Tu,s with general horizontal spin J, and shows how the operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$B_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Bu,s acts on it by shifting the parameter sequence. Below in Sect. 5, we consider specializations of Theorem 4.7 to simpler particle systems, which leads to known and new results. Most importantly, whereas the known results only applied to step initial conditions, the new results apply to stochastic particle systems started from a arbitrary initial condition.

Theorem 4.7

Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(\textbf{u},\textbf{s})\in \mathcal {T}\cap \mathcal {B}$$\end{document}(u,s)∈T∩B. Then4.7\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}} \hspace{1pt}B_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}} = B_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}} \hspace{1pt}T_{\textsf{sh}(\textbf{u}),\textsf{sh}(\textbf{s})}, \end{aligned}$$\end{document}Tu,sBu,s=Bu,sTsh(u),sh(s),where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textsf{sh}$$\end{document}sh is the shift (4.4). The same identity holds if all the operators in (4.7) are replaced (via the gap-particle transformation of Definition 2.4) by their corresponding counterparts acting on the space \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X.

Proof

This is simply an iteration of Proposition 4.2. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

Note that the intermediate summations, as in Remark 4.3, arising in the products in both sides of (4.7) are finite. Indeed, for any fixed \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{g}''\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g,g′′∈G there are only finitely many \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g′∈G such that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}(\textbf{g},\textbf{g}') \hspace{1pt}B_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}(\textbf{g}',\textbf{g}'')>0$$\end{document}Tu,s(g,g′)Bu,s(g′,g′′)>0. That is, with probability 1, the product of the Markov operators does not allow paths to run off to infinity if \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(\textbf{u},\textbf{s})\in \mathcal {T}\cap \mathcal {B}$$\end{document}(u,s)∈T∩B.

Application to q-Hahn TASEP and its Specializations

In this section we consider specializations of Theorem 4.7 to the q-Hahn TASEP [Pov13, Cor14], various q-TASEPs [SW98, BC14, BC15], and the usual TASEP. We recover the previously known results on parameter symmetry obtained in [PS22, Pet21], and extend them to arbitrary initial data. All Poisson-type limit transitions involved in this section are the same as in [Pet21], and therefore we only sketch the details of how discrete time Markov chains become continuous time Markov jump processes.

q-Hahn Boson and q-Hahn TASEP

Remark 5.1

Setting \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_i=u_i$$\end{document}si=ui is not the only way of making the cross vertex weights to take the simpler q-beta-binomial form. We do not focus on this case in the current Sect. 5 since this section is devoted to extending existing results from [PS22, Pet21] on q-Hahn TASEP and its specializations. Note that this result is formulated for the space \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X of particle configurations in \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathbb {Z}$$\end{document}Z. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

The swap operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\tilde{P}}^{(n),\textrm{qHahn}}_{s_{n-1},s_n}$$\end{document}P~sn-1,sn(n),qHahn preserves the step initial configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{y}=\textbf{x}_{step}$$\end{document}y=xstep due to the presence of the indicator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{1}_{g_n'\le g_n}$$\end{document}1gn′≤gn in (5.3). Thus, the swap operator does not randomize the initial configuration for the q-Hahn TASEP started with \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}_{step}$$\end{document}xstep. In the case of step initial data, Proposition 5.2 was proven in [Pet21] (up to matching notation \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\nu _i=s_{i-1}^2$$\end{document}νi=si-12) using exact formulas which are not readily available for general initial data. Finally, observe that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{P}^{(n),\textrm{qHahn}}_{s_{n-1},s_n}$$\end{document}P~sn-1,sn(n),qHahn becomes the identity operator when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_n=s_{n-1}$$\end{document}sn=sn-1, and the statement of Proposition 5.2 in this case is trivial (while still true).

One may also specialize Theorem 4.7 to the case of q-Hahn TASEP. The result is a shift operator which acts by removing the parameter \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_0$$\end{document}s0 if \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$|s_0|\ge |s_n|$$\end{document}|s0|≥|sn| for all \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$n\ge 1$$\end{document}n≥1. In a continuous time limit, this leads to an extension of [Pet21, Theorem 4.7] to general initial data. The original result [Pet21, Theorem 4.7] for the step initial data follows by observing that the q-Hahn specialization of the shift operator preserves \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}_{step}$$\end{document}xstep. To avoid cumbersome notation, in this paper we only consider the continuous limit for the case of q-TASEP, see Sects. 5.3 and 5.4 below.

Intertwining relation for geometric q-TASEP

Let us now consider the limit of the q-Hahn TASEP leading to the discrete time q-TASEP:5.5\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} s_n^2\rightarrow 0,\qquad \gamma s_n^2\rightarrow a_n\in (0,1),\qquad n=0,1,\ldots . \end{aligned}$$\end{document}sn2→0,γsn2→an∈(0,1),n=0,1,….This also implies that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_n^2/s_{k}^2\rightarrow a_n/a_k$$\end{document}sn2/sk2→an/ak. Under this limit, the q-Hahn TASEP turns into the discrete time geometric q-TASEP introduced in [BC15].
