Proof of Proposition 5.3

This is a specialization of Theorem 4.7 formulated in terms of particle systems. Note that the operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\tilde{T}}^{\textrm{qT}}_{\alpha ,r}$$\end{document}T~α,rqT is well-defined for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$a_k=\alpha r^k$$\end{document}ak=αrk, since \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$0<a_k<1$$\end{document}0<ak<1 for all k. Also, the shift operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{B}^{\textrm{qT}}_{r}$$\end{document}B~rqT is well-defined by Lemma 4.6 since \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$a_k>a_{k+1}$$\end{document}ak>ak+1 for all k, and the second condition in Definition 4.4 holds trivially if \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$u_i = s_i$$\end{document}ui=si for all i. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

Limit to continuous time q-TASEP

Let us now take a Poisson-type limit to continuous time for the geometric q-TASEP \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\tilde{T}}^{\textrm{qT}}_{\alpha ,r}$$\end{document}T~α,rqT. This is achieved by letting5.9\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \alpha \rightarrow 0, \qquad t=\lfloor (1-q)\textsf{t}/\alpha \rfloor , \end{aligned}$$\end{document}α→0,t=⌊(1-q)t/α⌋,where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textsf{t}\in \mathbb {R}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}t∈R≥0 is the new continuous time variable. Indeed, observe the expansion5.10\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \varphi _{q,\mu ,0}(h\mid g)= {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1+O(\mu ),& h=0;\\[4pt] \dfrac{1-q^g}{1-q}\hspace{1pt}\mu +O(\mu ^2),& h=1;\\[7pt] O(\mu ^2),& h\ge 1, \end{array}\right. } \qquad \qquad \mu \rightarrow 0. \end{aligned}$$\end{document}φq,μ,0(h∣g)=1+O(μ),h=0;[4pt]1-qg1-qμ+O(μ2),h=1;[7pt]O(μ2),h≥1,μ→0.This means that particles jump very rarely for small \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\alpha $$\end{document}α in discrete time. Moreover, when a particle jumps, it jumps by one with much higher probability than any other distance greater than one. Then, by speeding up the time, the discrete jumping distributions \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\varphi _{q,\alpha r^{n-1},0}$$\end{document}φq,αrn-1,0 (5.6) lead to independent exponential clocks. Therefore, under the resulting continuous time q-TASEP [BC14], each particle \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_n$$\end{document}xn has an independent exponential clock of rate \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$r^{n-1}\left( 1-q^{g_n} \right) $$\end{document}rn-11-qgn, where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_n=x_n-x_{n+1}-1$$\end{document}gn=xn-xn+1-1 (the factor \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$1-q$$\end{document}1-q in the rate in (5.10) is removed by the time scaling (5.9)). When the clock attached to the particle \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_n$$\end{document}xn rings, this particle jumps by 1 to the right. Note that when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$g_n=0$$\end{document}gn=0, the jump rate of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_n$$\end{document}xn is zero, which means that a particle cannot jump into an occupied location.

Remark 5.4

(TASEP specialization, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0). The continuous time q-TASEP with the sequence of speeds \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(1,r,r^2,\ldots )$$\end{document}(1,r,r2,…) turns into the TASEP with these speeds when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0. Under TASEP, each particle \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_n$$\end{document}xn has an independent exponential clock with rate \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$r^{n-1}$$\end{document}rn-1. When a clock rings, the corresponding particle jumps to the right by one, provided that the destination is unoccupied. Otherwise, the jump of the particle is blocked.

Moreover, in the case \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$r=1$$\end{document}r=1, we recover the well-known homogeneous continuous time TASEP in which the speeds of all particles are equal to 1.

Let us denote the continuous time Markov semigroup on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X corresponding to the continuous time q-TASEP with particle speeds \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(1,r,r^2,\ldots )$$\end{document}(1,r,r2,…) by \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\tilde{T}^{\textrm{qT}}_r(\textsf{t})\}_{\textsf{t}\in \mathbb {R}_{\ge 0}}$$\end{document}{T~rqT(t)}t∈R≥0. In the case \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$r=1$$\end{document}r=1, the process given by the semigroup \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{T}^{\textrm{qT}}_1(\textsf{t})$$\end{document}T~1qT(t) (which we will denote simply by \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\tilde{T}}^{\textrm{qT}}(\textsf{t})$$\end{document}T~qT(t)) is the homogeneous q-TASEP, where all particles have speeds equal to 1.

Taking the continuous time limit (5.9) in (5.8), we get the following intertwining relations for any \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 1}$$\end{document}m∈Z≥1:5.11\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \tilde{T}^{\textrm{qT}}_r(\textsf{t}) \bigl ( {\tilde{B}}^{\textrm{qT}}_{r} \bigr )^{m} = \bigl ( {\tilde{B}}^{\textrm{qT}}_{r} \bigr )^{m}\hspace{1pt}\tilde{T}^{\textrm{qT}}_r(r^{m}\hspace{1pt}\textsf{t}). \end{aligned}$$\end{document}T~rqT(t)(B~rqT)m=(B~rqT)mT~rqT(rmt).Indeed, shifting the sequence of speed parameters as \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(1,r,r^2,\ldots )\mapsto (r^m,r^{m+1},r^{m+2}, \ldots )$$\end{document}(1,r,r2,…)↦(rm,rm+1,rm+2,…) means slowing down all the particles by the factor \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$r^{m}$$\end{document}rm, which is equivalent to looking at the q-TASEP distribution at an earlier time \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$r^{m}\hspace{1pt}\textsf{t}$$\end{document}rmt.

Mapping q-TASEP back in time

We now aim to take one more Poisson-type limit in the intertwining relation (5.11). Let5.12\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} r= 1-\varepsilon ,\qquad m=\lfloor \tau /\varepsilon \rfloor ,\qquad \varepsilon \searrow 0, \end{aligned}$$\end{document}r=1-ε,m=⌊τ/ε⌋,ε↘0,where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tau \in \mathbb {R}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}τ∈R≥0 is a new continuous time parameter. We have the following interpretation for the expansion (5.13). Remark 5.5

In the TASEP specialization, when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0 (cf. Remark 5.4), the probabilities (5.14) define a uniform distribution. Therefore, under the backwards dynamics, when the clock of the particle \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x_n$$\end{document}xn rings (with rate \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$n(x_n-x_{n+1}-1)$$\end{document}n(xn-xn+1-1)), this particle selects one of the following locations\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \left\{ x_{n+1}+1,x_{n+1}+2,\ldots ,x_n-2,x_n-1 \right\} \end{aligned}$$\end{document}xn+1+1,xn+1+2,…,xn-2,xn-1uniformly at random, and instantaneously jumps into the selected location. Thus, setting \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0 turns the backwards q-TASEP dynamics \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\tilde{B}}^{\textrm{qT}}(\tau )$$\end{document}B~qT(τ) into the (inhomogeneous) backwards Hammersley process introduced in [PS22] (see Fig. 5 for an illustration).

Taking the Poisson-type limit (5.12) of the intertwining relation (5.11), we immediately obtain the main result of Sect. 5 (this is Theorem 1.7 from the Introduction):

Lax equation for q-TASEP and TASEP

We obtain a Lax type equation for the q-TASEP (and TASEP in the special case \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0), arising from identity (5.15) established in Theorem 5.6. Our computations in this subsection are informal, though we believe that the end results (5.17) and (5.18) become rigorous in appropriate spaces of functions. We believe that our Lax equation could be employed to study multipoint asymptotics of the q-TASEP and, in a scaling limit, lead to Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) or Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) type equations recently derived in [QR22] for the KPZ fixed point process [MQR21]. We leave the asymptotic analysis of the Lax equation to future work.

Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{\textsf{T}}$$\end{document}T~ and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{\textsf{B}}$$\end{document}B~ denote the infinitesimal generators of the q-TASEP and the backwards q-TASEP, respectively. Multiply both sides of (5.15) by \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{T}^{\textrm{qT}}(\textsf{t}-e^{-\tau }\textsf{t})$$\end{document}T~qT(t-e-τt) from the right. Identity (5.18) generalizes [Pet21, Proposition 5.3] (and also [PS22, Proposition 7.1] when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0) by allowing an arbitrary initial condition \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{y}$$\end{document}y. Indeed, if \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{y}=\textbf{x}_{step}$$\end{document}y=xstep, then \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{\textsf{B}} \hspace{1pt}\mathbb {E}_{\textbf{y}} \left[ F(\textbf{x}(\textsf{t})) \right] =0$$\end{document}B~EyF(x(t))=0 because \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{x}_{step}$$\end{document}xstep is an absorbing state for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{\textsf{B}}$$\end{document}B~. This preservation of measure was proven in [Pet21] using contour integral formulas available for the q-TASEP distribution with the step initial configuration, and for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0 in [PS22] using a different approach. Moreover, using duality, in [Pet21] it was shown that the process with the combined generator converges to its stationary distribution when started from an arbitrary initial configuration in \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X.

Application to Schur Vertex Model

The Schur vertex model studied in [KPS19] is the \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$J=1$$\end{document}J=1, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$q=0$$\end{document}q=0 specialization of the stochastic higher spin six vertex model \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t) defined in Sect. 2.3. The name “Schur” comes from the fact that some joint distributions in \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t) are expressed through the Schur processes [KPS19, Theorem 3.5]. This model can be equivalently reformulated as a certain corner growth [KPS19, Section 1.2], and is also equivalent to the generalized TASEP of [DPPP12] and [Pov13], which appeared (in the form of tandem queues and first passage percolation models) already in [Woe05] and [Mar09]. Here we outline the specialization of the general shift operator from Sect. 4.2 to this model. We also observe that in contrast with the q-Hahn TASEP and its specializations, in the Schur vertex model the shift operator does not preserve the distinguished initial configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}_{step}$$\end{document}gstep.

The Schur vertex model scales to a version of the TASEP in continuous inhomogeneous space [KPS19, Theorem 2.7]. It would be interesting to see how the shift operators behave under this scaling, but we do not pursue this analysis here.

Schur vertex model

The Schur vertex model depends on the parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$u_i,s_i$$\end{document}ui,si as in (2.17). Shift operator for the Schur vertex model

Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$B^{\textrm{Schur}}_{\nu ,\textbf{a}}$$\end{document}Bν,aSchur denote the Markov shift operator (Definition 4.5) for the Schur vertex model. Proposition 6.1

Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\nu \in (0,1)$$\end{document}ν∈(0,1) and the parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$a_n\ge 0$$\end{document}an≥0 be uniformly bounded from above and satisfy (6.2). Then6.3\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} T^{\textrm{Schur}}_{\nu ,\textbf{a}}\hspace{1pt}B^{\textrm{Schur}}_{\nu ,\textbf{a}} = B^{\textrm{Schur}}_{\nu ,\textbf{a}}\hspace{1pt}T^{\textrm{Schur}}_{\nu ,\textsf{sh}(\textbf{a})}, \end{aligned}$$\end{document}Tν,aSchurBν,aSchur=Bν,aSchurTν,sh(a)Schur,where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textsf{sh}$$\end{document}sh is the shift of the sequence \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{a}=(a_0,a_1,a_2,\ldots )$$\end{document}a=(a0,a1,a2,…) as in (4.4).

In contrast with the q-Hahn TASEP and its specializations considered in Sect. 5 and in the previous papers [PS22] and [Pet21], the shift operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$B^{\textrm{Schur}}_{\nu ,\textbf{a}}$$\end{document}Bν,aSchur, for the Schur vertex model, does not preserve the distinguished empty configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}_{step}\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}gstep∈G:

Proposition 6.2

Let the parameters \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{a_n \}$$\end{document}{an} satisfy (6.2). Part II Bijectivisation and Rewriting History

In the second part, we describe how the intertwining relations obtained in the first part lead to couplings between trajectories of the stochastic vertex model (and the corresponding exclusion process) with different sequences of parameters. The passage from intertwining relations to couplings, a “bijectivisation”, is by now a well-known technique that originated in [DF90] and was later developed in the context of integrable stochastic particle systems in [BF14, BG09, BP16b, BP19]. Here, we apply a bijectivisation in a new setting leading to couplings of probability measures on trajectories under time evolution of integrable stochastic systems.

Bijectivisation and Coupling of Trajectories. General Constructions

In this section, we return to the general setup of the fused stochastic higher spin six vertex model as in Sects. 2 to 4. We construct couplings between measures on trajectories of the stochastic higher spin six vertex model with different sequences of parameters by applying a bijectivisation [BP19] (also called a “probabilistic bijection”, e.g., see [AF21]) to the Yang-Baxter equation and iterating it. This section focuses on a general discussion which does not rely on any particular choice of a bijectivisation of the Yang-Baxter equation. In further sections, we consider the simplest, i.e. independent, bijectivisation in a subfamily of vertex models. This subfamily is still quite general and, in particular, includes q-TASEP and TASEP.

Bijectivisation of summation identities

We begin by recalling the basic notion of a bijectivisation for a summation identity with finitely many terms, see [BP19, Section 2]. Let A, B be two disjoint finite sets. Also, introduce a positive weight function w(x) for each element \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$x \in A \cup B$$\end{document}x∈A∪B so that the following identity holds:7.1\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \sum _{a\in A}w(a) = \sum _{b\in B}w(b). \end{aligned}$$\end{document}∑a∈Aw(a)=∑b∈Bw(b).In particular, identity (7.1) defines probability distributions on the sets A and B with probability weights proportional to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{w(a)\}_{a\in A}$$\end{document}{w(a)}a∈A and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{w(b)\}_{b\in B}$$\end{document}{w(b)}b∈B, respectively. A bijectivisation is a coupling between these two probability distributions, expressed via conditional probabilities.

More precisely, a bijectivisation is a family of forward and backward transition probabilities \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$p^{\textrm{fwd}}(a \rightarrow b)\ge 0$$\end{document}pfwd(a→b)≥0, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$p^{\textrm{bwd}}(b \rightarrow a)\ge 0$$\end{document}pbwd(b→a)≥0, for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$a\in A$$\end{document}a∈A, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$b\in B$$\end{document}b∈B, satisfying the following stochasticity and detailed balance equation:7.2\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \begin{aligned}&\sum _{b \in B} p^{\textrm{fwd}}(a \rightarrow b) = 1 \quad \forall a \in A, \qquad \qquad \sum _{a \in A} p^{\textrm{bwd}}(b \rightarrow a) = 1 \quad \forall b \in B. \\&\hspace{35pt} w(a)\, p^{\textrm{fwd}}(a \rightarrow b) = w(b)\, p^{\textrm{bwd}}(b \rightarrow a), \qquad \forall a\in A,\ b\in B. \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$\end{document}∑b∈Bpfwd(a→b)=1∀a∈A,∑a∈Apbwd(b→a)=1∀b∈B.w(a)pfwd(a→b)=w(b)pbwd(b→a),∀a∈A,b∈B.For general sets A and B, a bijectivisation exists and it is not unique. However, in the special case when the cardinality of the sets A or B, i.e. |A| or |B|, is equal to 1, a bijectivisation is unique. For instance, when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$|A|=1$$\end{document}|A|=1 and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$A=\left\{ a_0 \right\} $$\end{document}A=a0, we have\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} p^{\textrm{fwd}}(a_0 \rightarrow b)=\frac{w(b)}{w(a_0)}, \qquad p^{\textrm{bwd}}(b \rightarrow a_0)=1, \qquad \forall b\in B. \end{aligned}$$\end{document}pfwd(a0→b)=w(b)w(a0),pbwd(b→a0)=1,∀b∈B.In the case when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$|A|=|B|=2$$\end{document}|A|=|B|=2, the dimension of the space of all possible solutions to the linear equations (7.2) is equal to one, meaning that there is a one-parameter family of bijectivizations for this case.

Remark 7.1

(Bijectivisation with infinitely many paths). We tacitly included the case of infinitely many paths \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_2=j_3=+\infty $$\end{document}i2=j3=+∞ (arising at the left boundary of the stochastic higher spin six vertex model, see Sect. 3.5) into the notation (7.4). In this case, the range of the down transition probability (i.e. the set of possible values of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$(\infty ,k_2')$$\end{document}(∞,k2′)) is always finite. \infty ] \end{aligned}$$\end{document}p∗,j1↑[(∞,k2′)→(∞,k3)∣∞,i3,j2,∞](“\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$*$$\end{document}∗” means that there is no dependence on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_1$$\end{document}i1) may be infinite, since both \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} Throughout the rest of this section, we assume that a well-defined bijectivisation at the left boundary exists. In considering explicit bijectivisations for the present paper, we restrict our attention to models with \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$J=1$$\end{document}J=1 and, thus, the issue of an infinite range of the up transition probability does not arise.

In the current Sect. 7, we explain the general framework for a bijectivisation and couplings of measures on trajectories of stochastic vertex models. We do not pursue an explicit computation of possible transition probabilities \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$p^{\downarrow }_{i_1,j_1}$$\end{document}pi1,j1↓ and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$p^{\uparrow }_{i_1,j_1}$$\end{document}pi1,j1↑ in the fully general case when all three vertex weights entering the Yang-Baxter equation have a q-hypergeometric form. Below in Sect. 8, we focus on a, still rather general, subfamily of vertex models for which the cross vertex weights factorize and become q-beta-binomial as in Sect. 3.4. Moreover, we set \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$J=1$$\end{document}J=1 in the weights \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$L^{(J)}_{u_i,s_i}$$\end{document}Lui,si(J), which forces \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$i_1,j_1$$\end{document}i1,j1 to be either zero or one. For this subfamily, an explicit treatment of a bijectivisation is accessible.

Down and up transitions on vertex model configurations

Recall the space \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {G}$$\end{document}G whose elements encode vertical paths crossing a given horizontal slice in the stochastic higher spin six vertex model, see Sect. 2.3. Recall the transition operator of the stochastic vertex model \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}$$\end{document}Tu,s (Sect. 2.3) and the swap operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}_{z,s_1,s_2}$$\end{document}Pz,s1,s2(n) ((Sect. 4.1). These operators satisfy a (quasi-)computation relation (Proposition 4.2) which follows from the Yang-Baxter equation. Here we employ bijectivisation of this intertwining relation to define up and down transitions on vertex model configurations.

Fix \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$n\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 1}$$\end{document}n∈Z≥1 and abbreviate throughout the rest of this section:7.5\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} P^{(n)}=P^{(n)}_{u_n/u_{n-1},s_{n-1},s_n}, \qquad T=T_{\textbf{u},\textbf{s}}, \qquad T_{\sigma }= T_{\sigma \textbf{u},\sigma \textbf{s}}, \end{aligned}$$\end{document}P(n)=Pun/un-1,sn-1,sn(n),T=Tu,s,Tσ=Tσu,σs,where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\sigma $$\end{document}σ is an arbitrary permutation from the infinite symmetric group (that is, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\sigma $$\end{document}σ acts on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}Z≥0 by fixing all but finitely many points). The intertwining relation from Proposition 4.2 is7.6\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} TP^{(n)}=P^{(n)}T_{\sigma _{n-1}}, \end{aligned}$$\end{document}TP(n)=P(n)Tσn-1,see Fig. 13, left, for an illustration. Here \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\sigma _{n-1}=(n-1,n)$$\end{document}σn-1=(n-1,n) is an elementary transposition. Recall that we are writing products of Markov operators as acting on measures, cf. Remark 4.3.

Lemma 7.4

Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{d}\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g,d∈G and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$M>1+\max \left\{ l\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 1}:g_l>0 \ \text {or}\ d_l>0 \right\} $$\end{document}M>1+maxl∈Z≥1:gl>0ordl>0. Then7.14\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} B(\textbf{g},\textbf{d}) = \prod _{m=1}^{M} P^{(0,m)}(\textbf{g}_{[m-1]},\textbf{g}_{[m]}) \end{aligned}$$\end{document}B(g,d)=∏m=1MP(0,m)(g[m-1],g[m])and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}=\textbf{g}_{[M]}$$\end{document}d=g[M].

Lemma 4.6 essentially shows that for fixed \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}$$\end{document}g, the sum of (7.14) over all \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}$$\end{document}d is equal to 1. Since M depends on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}$$\end{document}d in (7.14), Lemma 7.4 does not imply Lemma 4.6.

Proof of Lemma 7.4

For all \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\ge M$$\end{document}m≥M, we have \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$h_m=0$$\end{document}hm=0 by the lower bound on M. Hence, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}_{[m-1]}=\textbf{g}_{[m]}$$\end{document}g[m-1]=g[m] for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\ge M$$\end{document}m≥M. In particular, for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\ge M$$\end{document}m≥M, we have \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(0,m)}(\textbf{g}_{[m-1]},\textbf{g}_{[m]}) = \textbf{1}_{\textbf{g}_{[m]}=\textbf{g}_{[m-1]}}$$\end{document}P(0,m)(g[m-1],g[m])=1g[m]=g[m-1] since the path configuration, as in Fig. 11, is empty to the right of location M. Thus, we may truncate the infinite product of swap operators \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(0,m)}$$\end{document}P(0,m) that define the operator B, see (4.6), to the product of the swap operators \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(0,m)}$$\end{document}P(0,m) in (7.14). Additionally, note that the \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}_{[m]}$$\end{document}g[m]’s stabilize to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}$$\end{document}d. This completes the proof.

For \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}',\textbf{d}'$$\end{document}g′,d′ with \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$B(\textbf{g}',\textbf{d}')\ne 0$$\end{document}B(g′,d′)≠0 and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 0}$$\end{document}m∈Z≥0, define \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'_{[m]}$$\end{document}g[m]′ in the same way as in (7.13)–(7.12). The construction of the tower of intertwining relations given in Fig. 14 follows from the representation (7.14) of the shift operators together with (7.6). Note, in particular, that the tower is finite since the \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}_{[m]}$$\end{document}g[m] and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'_{[m]}$$\end{document}g[m]′ stabilize as is shown below.

Lemma 7.5

Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{g}',\textbf{d},\textbf{d}'\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g,g′,d,d′∈G, and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$M>1+\max \left\{ l\in \mathbb {Z}_{\ge 1}:\max (g_l,g_l',d_l,d_l')>0 \right\} $$\end{document}M>1+maxl∈Z≥1:max(gl,gl′,dl,dl′)>0. Then, for any \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\ge M$$\end{document}m≥M, we have7.15\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} T_{\sigma _{m-2}\sigma _{m-3}\ldots \sigma _1\sigma _0 } (\textbf{g}_{[m-1]},\textbf{g}'_{[m-1]})= T_{\sigma _{m-1}\sigma _{m-2}\sigma _{m-3}\ldots \sigma _1\sigma _0 } (\textbf{g}_{[m]},\textbf{g}'_{[m]}), \end{aligned}$$\end{document}Tσm-2σm-3…σ1σ0(g[m-1],g[m-1]′)=Tσm-1σm-2σm-3…σ1σ0(g[m],g[m]′),and7.16\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} \begin{aligned} D^{(0,m)}(\textbf{g}'_{[m-1]}\rightarrow \textbf{g}_{[m]}\mid \textbf{g}_{[m-1]},\textbf{g}_{[m]}')&= \textbf{1}_{\textbf{g}_{[m]}=\textbf{g}_{[m-1]}}, \\ U^{(0,m)}(\textbf{g}_{[m]}\rightarrow \textbf{g}'_{[m-1]}\mid \textbf{g}_{[m-1]},\textbf{g}_{[m]}')&= \textbf{1}_{\textbf{g}'_{[m-1]}=\textbf{g}_{[m]}'}. \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$\end{document}D(0,m)(g[m-1]′→g[m]∣g[m-1],g[m]′)=1g[m]=g[m-1],U(0,m)(g[m]→g[m-1]′∣g[m-1],g[m]′)=1g[m-1]′=g[m]′.

Proof

Observe that the transfer matrices \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\sigma _{m-2}\ldots \sigma _1\sigma _0 }$$\end{document}Tσm-2…σ1σ0 and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\sigma _{m-1}\sigma _{m-2}\ldots \sigma _1\sigma _0 }$$\end{document}Tσm-1σm-2…σ1σ0 differ only by the location of the parameter \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_0$$\end{document}s0. Moreover, for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\ge M$$\end{document}m≥M, the action of the these transfer matrices on the configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}_{[m]}$$\end{document}g[m] does not depend on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$s_0$$\end{document}s0 since the configuration is empty to the right of M. Therefore, the action is the same. This proves (7.15).

Next, notice that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(0,m)}$$\end{document}P(0,m) acts as identity on our elements for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m\ge M$$\end{document}m≥M, see the proof of Lemma 7.4. Then, along with (7.15), this implies that the detailed balance equation for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$D^{(0,m)},U^{(0,m)}$$\end{document}D(0,m),U(0,m) has a unique solution given by (7.16). This completes the proof. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

Definition 7.6

[Down operator for shift]. Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{g}',\textbf{d}'\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g,g′,d′∈G be such that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T(\textbf{g},\textbf{g}')B(\textbf{g}',\textbf{d}') \ne 0$$\end{document}T(g,g′)B(g′,d′)≠0. The down Markov operator corresponding to the shift operator B is defined as follows:7.17\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} D^{\bullet }(\textbf{g}'\rightarrow \textbf{d}\mid \textbf{g},\textbf{d}') :=\prod _{m=1}^{\infty } D^{(0,m)}(\textbf{g}'_{[m-1]}\rightarrow \textbf{g}_{[m]}\mid \textbf{g}_{[m-1]},\textbf{g}_{[m]}'), \qquad \textbf{d}=\lim _{m\rightarrow +\infty }\textbf{g}_{[m]}\in \mathscr {G}.\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$\end{document}D∙(g′→d∣g,d′):=∏m=1∞D(0,m)(g[m-1]′→g[m]∣g[m-1],g[m]′),d=limm→+∞g[m]∈G.Due to Lemma 7.5, the product is actually finite and the limit stabilizes. See Figs. 13 and 14 for an illustration

Note that for any \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{g}',\textbf{d}'\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g,g′,d′∈G, there are only finitely many \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}d∈G for which (7.17) is nonzero. This is due to the fact that there are only finitely many \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}$$\end{document}d for which \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textsf{sh}}(\textbf{d},\textbf{d}')\ne 0$$\end{document}Tsh(d,d′)≠0, see the desired detailed balance equation (7.10).

Definition 7.7

[Up operator for shift]. Let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{d},\textbf{d}'\in \mathscr {G}$$\end{document}g,d,d′∈G be such that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$B(\textbf{g},\textbf{d}) T_\textsf{sh}(\textbf{d},\textbf{d}')\ne 0$$\end{document}B(g,d)Tsh(d,d′)≠0. The up Markov operator corresponding to the shift operator B is defined as follows:7.18\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} U^{\bullet }(\textbf{d}\rightarrow \textbf{g}'\mid \textbf{g},\textbf{d}') :=\prod _{m=1}^{\infty } U^{(0,m)}(\textbf{g}_{[m]}\rightarrow \textbf{g}'_{[m-1]}\mid \textbf{g}_{[m-1]},\textbf{g}_{[m]}'), \qquad \textbf{g}'=\textbf{g}'_{[0]}\in \mathscr {G}.\nonumber \\ \end{aligned}$$\end{document}U∙(d→g′∣g,d′):=∏m=1∞U(0,m)(g[m]→g[m-1]′∣g[m-1],g[m]′),g′=g[0]′∈G.Due to Lemma 7.5, the product is actually finite. See Figs. 13 and 14 for an illustration.

We assume that the bijectivisation at the left boundary is well-defined, so that the whole up operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$U^{\bullet }$$\end{document}U∙ is also well-defined. In contrast with the down operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$D^{\bullet }$$\end{document}D∙, in (7.18), the number of possible outcomes \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'$$\end{document}g′ for any fixed \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g},\textbf{d},\textbf{d}'$$\end{document}g,d,d′ may be infinite. These infinitely many choices arise at the left boundary, for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$m=1$$\end{document}m=1, as explained in Remark 7.1.

One readily sees that the operators \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$D^{\bullet }$$\end{document}D∙ and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$U^{\bullet }$$\end{document}U∙ from Definitions 7.6 and 7.7 satisfy the detailed balance equation (7.10) involving the shift operator B and the stochastic higher spin six vertex model transfer matrices T and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\textsf{sh}}$$\end{document}Tsh. This follows directly from the detailed balance equations for the Markov swap operators \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$D^{(0,n)}$$\end{document}D(0,n) and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$U^{(0,n)}$$\end{document}U(0,n) given by (7.11).

Remark 7.8

Here, and in Sect. 7.3, we argued in terms of the space \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {G}$$\end{document}G of vertex model configurations. Note that we may define corresponding down and up Markov operators to act on the space \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X of exclusion process configurations via the gap-particle transformation (Definition 2.4). Following our convention so far, we use the notation \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tilde{D}^{(n)},{\tilde{D}}^{(0,n)},{\tilde{D}}^{\bullet }$$\end{document}D~(n),D~(0,n),D~∙, and so on, to denote these operators acting on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathscr {X}$$\end{document}X.

Coupling of measures on trajectories via rewriting history

We couple together trajectories of two instances of the stochastic higher spin six vertex model with different parameters through the use of the down and up Markov operators defined in Sects. 7.3 and 7.4. Here, we only consider this construction for the swap operator \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}$$\end{document}P(n) and the operators \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$D^{(n)},U^{(n)}$$\end{document}D(n),U(n) from Sect. 7.3. The couplings involving the shift operator B work very similarly, and they will be discussed in a continuous time limit in Sect. 10 below.

Sequentially in the order \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t=1,2,\ldots ,M $$\end{document}t=1,2,…,M, let \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'(t)$$\end{document}g′(t) be sampled from 7.21\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned} U^{(n)}(\textbf{d}(t-1)\rightarrow \textbf{g}'(t)\mid \textbf{g}'(t-1),\textbf{d}(t)), \end{aligned}$$\end{document}U(n)(d(t-1)→g′(t)∣g′(t-1),d(t)), where, by agreement, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}'(0)=\hat{\textbf{g}}$$\end{document}g′(0)=g^. Then, the joint distribution of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\textbf{g}'(t)\}_{0\le t\le M}$$\end{document}{g′(t)}0≤t≤M is equal to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\mathfrak {T}$$\end{document}T.

Proof

The results follow by iterating the detailed balance equation (7.8) involving \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T,T_{\sigma _{n-1}}$$\end{document}T,Tσn-1, and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}$$\end{document}P(n). Moreover, by the Markov property, it suffices to consider joint distributions at adjacent time moments \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t,t+1$$\end{document}t,t+1, and use induction in t. This induction is descending or ascending in the first or the second part, respectively. See Fig. 15 for an illustration of the notation employed throughout the proof. We give more details below.

Consider the first part. Inductively, we show that the transition probability \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$ \textbf{d}'(t) \rightarrow \textbf{d}'(t+1)$$\end{document}d′(t)→d′(t+1) is equal to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\sigma _{n-1}} (\textbf{d}'(t), \textbf{d}'(t+1))$$\end{document}Tσn-1(d′(t),d′(t+1)) if the transition probability for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t) \rightarrow \textbf{g}(t+1)$$\end{document}g(t)→g(t+1) is equal to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T( \textbf{g}(t), \textbf{g}(t+1))$$\end{document}T(g(t),g(t+1)). Additionally, for the induction argument, we show that the transition probability for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t) \rightarrow \textbf{d}'(t)$$\end{document}g(t)→d′(t) is equal to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}(\textbf{g}(t), \textbf{d}'(t))$$\end{document}P(n)(g(t),d′(t)) if the transition probability for \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t+1) \rightarrow \textbf{d}'(t+1)$$\end{document}g(t+1)→d′(t+1) is equal to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}(\textbf{g}(t+1), \textbf{d}'(t+1))$$\end{document}P(n)(g(t+1),d′(t+1)). We start the induction by noting that the conditions are true for the first step when \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$t+1 = M$$\end{document}t+1=M by assumption. In the following, we carry out the computations for the induction step.

Let us assume that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t) is known. That is, the following computations are conditioned on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t). Then, we have the following chain of expressions for the joint distribution of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}'(t),\textbf{d}'(t+1)$$\end{document}d′(t),d′(t+1) conditioned on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t):\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\begin{aligned}&{\mathbb {P}}\left( \textbf{d}'(t+1),\textbf{d}'(t) \mid \textbf{g}(t) \right) \\&= {\mathbb {P}}\left( \textbf{d}'(t) \mid \textbf{g}(t)\right) \hspace{1pt}{\mathbb {P}}\left( \textbf{d}'(t+1) \mid \textbf{d}'(t), \textbf{g}(t) \right) \\&= \sum _{\textbf{g}(t+1)}T(\textbf{g}(t),\textbf{g}(t+1)) \hspace{1pt}P^{(n)}(\textbf{g}(t+1),\textbf{d}'(t+1)) \hspace{1pt}D^{(n)}(\textbf{g}(t+1)\rightarrow \textbf{d}'(t)\mid \textbf{g}(t),\textbf{d}'(t+1))\\&=\sum _{\textbf{g}(t+1)}P^{(n)}(\textbf{g}(t),\textbf{d}'(t)) \hspace{1pt}T_{\sigma _{n-1}}(\textbf{d}'(t),\textbf{d}'(t+1)) U^{(n)}(\textbf{d}'(t) \rightarrow From the identity above we see that the conditional distribution of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}'(t+1)$$\end{document}d′(t+1) given \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}'(t)$$\end{document}d′(t) is \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$T_{\sigma _{n-1}}(\textbf{d}'(t),\textbf{d}'(t+1))$$\end{document}Tσn-1(d′(t),d′(t+1)), which is independent of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{g}(t)$$\end{document}g(t). The second part is proven similarly, with a simplification that we do not need to condition the computations on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}(t)$$\end{document}d(t) due to the other direction of the Markov step \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}$$\end{document}P(n). This completes the proof. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\square $$\end{document}□

Definition 7.10

(Markov operators for rewriting history). Fix a trajectory \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\textbf{g}(t)\}_{0\le t\le M}$$\end{document}{g(t)}0≤t≤M of the stochastic higher spin six vertex model with some initial data \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\hat{\textbf{g}}$$\end{document}g^, and also fix an arbitrary configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\textbf{d}'(M)$$\end{document}d′(M) at the final time such that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}(\textbf{g}(M),\textbf{d}'(M))\ne 0$$\end{document}P(n)(g(M),d′(M))≠0. Similarly, fix a trajectory \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\{\textbf{d}(t)\}_{0\le t\le M}$$\end{document}{d(t)}0≤t≤M with some initial data \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\hat{\textbf{d}}$$\end{document}d^, and fix an arbitrary configuration \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\hat{\textbf{g}}$$\end{document}g^ such that \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$P^{(n)}(\hat{\textbf{g}},\hat{\textbf{d}})\ne 0$$\end{document}P(n)(g^,d^)≠0.
